features.spec: Read only `conversation` (turns formatted '[speaker]: text'). Return 1 if the text shows at least one multi-turn reply interaction: at least two successive turns in which a later turn evidently responds to the content of an earlier reply/comment (e.g., addresses or rebuts what the previous speaker said, answers their question), i.e. a chain of reply-to-reply rather than independent top-level comments addressed to the OP's post. Do not infer reply links from speaker order or repeated speaker names alone; require content evidence. Return 0 if turns are only independent comments or no such chain is evident. Empty text -> 0; missing/malformed -> null. Do not treat OP view-change/delta-award announcements or outcome reports as evidence of the interaction; ignore such turns when judging.

features.name: arg_self_meta_platform_or_status
features.definition: Does the OP's argument contain explicit self-referential meta-commentary about platform mechanics or the author's own status?
features.spec: Read only the `argument` text (OP's argument body; not title). Return 1 if the OP's own text explicitly comments on itself/their own posting in terms of platform mechanics (e.g., subreddit rules, delta system/mechanics, moderation, posting/formatting/edit features, votes/karma, how the post was submitted) or on the author's own status (e.g., being new/long-time user, account status, credentials, who they are as poster). Return 0 if no such commentary. Exclude OP view-change/delta-award announcements, post-outcome resolution updates (e.g., 'EDIT: view changed, delta awarded') and reports of the outcome; these do not count as evidence. Generic discussion of platform rules not about the OP's own post/status is not self-referential. Quoted text from others does not count unless the OP adopts it. If argument is missing or malformed return null; empty string returns 0.

features.name: post_score_below_median
features.definition: Is the post's observed score below the median post score across the supplied rows?
features.spec: s = pd.to_numeric(df['post_score'], errors='coerce'); med = s.median(); df['post_score_below_median'] = (s < med).astype('float').where(s.notna()) ; output 1 if post_score is strictly below the median of post_score over all supplied rows, 0 if equal to or above the median, null if post_score is missing or non-numeric. Uses the supplied post_score value as is.

features.name: argument_has_first_person_singular
features.definition: Does the original argument text contain at least one explicit first-person singular pronoun (I, me, my, mine, myself)?
features.spec: Read only df['argument']. If missing/non-string return null; empty string gives 0. Normalise curly apostrophes to ' then: df['argument'].apply(lambda s: None if not isinstance(s,str) else int(bool(re.search(r"\b(?:i|me|my|mine|myself)\b|\bi'(?:m|ve|d|ll)\b", s.replace('’',"'"), flags=re.I)))). Counts any occurrence anywhere in the argument, including within quotations (raw mechanical match, no semantic filtering). Title and comments are not read.

features.name: counterargument_cognitive_complexity
features.definition: What is the average cognitive complexity (differentiation of multiple considerations/perspectives and their integration) across the counter-argument comments?
features.spec: Parse OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than the OP). Rate each comment's own reasoning for cognitive complexity on a 1-4 scale: 1 = simple single assertion, no reasoning or only bare opinion; 2 = gives one line of reasoning or evidence without considering alternatives; 3 = differentiates several considerations, perspectives, cases or conditions; 4 = differentiates AND integrates multiple perspectives/considerations (e.g., weighs trade-offs, conditional or nuanced reasoning, reconciles tensions). Judge the commenter's own reasoning; quoted text counts only if the commenter adopts or engages with it. Ignore any OP view-change/delta-award announcements, thanks-for-changing-my-view, post-outcome updates or reports of the outcome; do not treat them as evidence of complexity. Do not reward length alone. Output the arithmetic mean of the per-comment ratings across all comments (float 1-4). Empty list gives null; malformed/missing input gives null.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument includes explicit comparisons to established scientific or historical norms are associated with lower view change than those without such comparisons.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions whose argument has arg_compares_to_science_history_norms=1 have the same view-change (delta) rate as those with 0.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions whose argument has arg_compares_to_science_history_norms=1 have lower view-change (delta) than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: Presence interpreted as binary. Uses current argument text, which may include edits or outcome announcements (excluded from semantic judgment but timing not recoverable). Association only; OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Arguments expressing explicit fear of social rejection or isolation are associated with lower view-change rates than arguments stating beliefs without emotional self-defense.
hypotheses.h0: Rows with arg_expresses_fear_of_social_rejection and rows with arg_states_beliefs_without_emotional_self_defense have the same view-change rate.
hypotheses.h1: Rows with arg_expresses_fear_of_social_rejection have a lower view-change rate than rows with arg_states_beliefs_without_emotional_self_defense.
hypotheses.note: The claim compares fear group (A) with a named no-self-defense group (B). In the A+B model each coefficient is relative to the neither group, so beta_A is not beta_A - beta_B, and no single coefficient expresses the requested contrast; term=null. Overlap and neither cases are preserved (neither = other self-defense without social fear, etc.). Argument text is current text and may contain edits/outcome announcements; no pre-outcome snapshot is available. Measurements are semantic LLM judgments of linguistic expression, not measured traits. Associations only.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Counter-arguments that cite specific, functioning institutional precedents are associated with a higher probability of view change than those relying on abstract normative principles.
hypotheses.h0: There is no difference in the probability of view change between discussions whose counter-arguments cite functioning institutional precedents and those relying on abstract normative principles.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with counter-arguments citing specific functioning institutional precedents (any_comment_cites_functioning_institutional_precedent) have a higher probability of view change than those relying on abstract normative principles (any_comment_relies_on_abstract_normative_principles).
hypotheses.note: The claim is a comparison of precedent-citing vs abstract-principle comments. The two binary features overlap and can both be 0 or both be 1. With the additive formula, no single coefficient equals beta_precedent minus beta_abstract, so term=null; no difference score was invented. Operational assumptions: presence (any comment) is used as no quantity was specified; the comparison is at discussion level. Source risk: OC_comments may contain outcome announcements; the prompts exclude them. Associations only.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions featuring longer precomputed log-transformed discussion length are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: supplied_log_length has no association with the likelihood that the OP changed their view (delta).
hypotheses.h1: Higher supplied_log_length is associated with a higher likelihood that the OP changed their view (delta).
hypotheses.note: Uses the supplied log_length column as given; its construction, source text, log base and timing relative to the outcome are undocumented, and it is not equated with argument word count. It may include post-outcome text. OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model; the result is an association, not a causal effect.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains explicit admissions of uncertainty are associated with a higher probability of view change than those asserting absolute certainty.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions whose original argument admits uncertainty (`argument_admits_uncertainty`) have the same probability of view change as those asserting absolute certainty (`argument_asserts_absolute_certainty`).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with `argument_admits_uncertainty` have a higher probability of view change than those with `argument_asserts_absolute_certainty`.
hypotheses.note: The claim compares uncertainty-admitting arguments with absolute-certainty arguments. In the chosen formula each coefficient is relative to the omitted baseline (neither), so neither coefficient equals beta_A - beta_B; no single coefficient expresses the requested contrast, hence term=null. Overlap and neither cases exist and are preserved. Both features read current argument text, which may contain edits or outcome announcements (contamination/timing risk); semantic prompts exclude those announcements. Association only, not causal.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Counter-arguments frequently challenging multiple distinct factual premises within the argument are positively associated with view change.
hypotheses.h0: distinct_factual_premises_challenged_count has no association with view change (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Higher distinct_factual_premises_challenged_count is associated with a higher probability of view change (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: Operational assumption: "frequently challenging multiple distinct factual premises" is measured as the count of distinct OP factual premises challenged by at least one comment; no threshold of "multiple" is imposed (a linear count term). Comment list order and timing are unknown. Argument text and comments may contain outcome announcements/edits; the prompt excludes them as evidence, but the current text is not a pre-outcome snapshot. Fact vs. value premise classification is judged by the annotator. OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model; association only, not causal.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains fewer counter-argument responses are associated with a lower likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: oc_comment_count has no association with the likelihood that the OP changed their view (delta).
hypotheses.h1: Higher oc_comment_count is associated with a higher likelihood of the OP changing their view (fewer comments, lower likelihood).
hypotheses.note: "Fewer counter-argument responses" is operationalized as a lower count of comments in OC_comments (available comments by other users), tested linearly with OLS (linear probability). The list may be a sampled or truncated subset of all responses, and it may include comments made after or because of a view change; its timing is unknown. This is an association, not a causal effect.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions with at least three distinct counter-arguments in the posted comments are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.

hypotheses.h1: Discussions with has_three_plus_counterarguments=1 have a higher likelihood of OP view change than those with fewer than three.
hypotheses.note: Operational assumptions: "distinct" means non-duplicated argumentative points, counted across available comments only (list is not necessarily complete or chronological). OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model. Comments may include outcome announcements; the prompt excludes them as evidence. Association only.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original post title uses absolute certainty markers are associated with a lower likelihood of the original poster changing their view.

hypotheses.h1: Titles with title_has_absolute_certainty_marker=1 are associated with a lower likelihood of the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.note: Presence of any absolute certainty marker is assumed (no count/intensity specified). The marker list is illustrative; the judgment is semantic. Titles are the OP's current text and could in principle contain edited content, though titles rarely include outcome announcements. Association only, not causal.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where original posts explicitly invite critique or use tentative language are associated with higher view-change rates than those using absolute, definitive declarations.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions whose OP invites critique or uses tentative language (`op_invites_critique_or_tentative`) have the same view-change rate as those whose OP uses absolute declarations (`op_uses_absolute_declarations`).
hypotheses.h1: View-change rates are higher for OPs with `op_invites_critique_or_tentative` than for OPs with `op_uses_absolute_declarations`.
hypotheses.note: The claim compares two named groups, so the required contrast is beta_invite minus beta_absolute, which is not a single coefficient in this formula. I did not build a difference score, so term is null. Both measurements are kept; overlap and neither cases are possible. Measures use current OP text (title and argument), which may include edits or outcome announcements and is not guaranteed pre-outcome. The prompt specs exclude outcome announcements. Hedging and absolutism are judged by an LLM with no fixed scale.

hypotheses.note: Unspecified quantity treated as presence in at least one comment. OLS on binary delta (linear probability model); association only. hypotheses.hypothesis: Counterarguments containing measured, logical reasoning are positively associated with the original poster changing their mind compared to those containing emotional aggression in ChangeMyView discussions.

In the OLS formula the two coefficients are separate and no single term expresses that contrast, so term=null; no difference score is invented. Overlap (both present) and neither cases exist. Presence (any comment) is assumed since no quantity was specified. Comments are unordered; current text may contain outcome announcements (excluded semantically). Associations only, not causal.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly quote and refute specific factual claims in the original post are associated with higher rates of view change.

Factual vs. opinion claims is a judgment call.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly validate the original poster's personal dignity or effort before introducing corrective logic are associated with higher view-change rates than purely logical refutations.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments introduce concrete, external factual analogies are associated with higher view-change rates than those relying solely on abstract logical refutation.

hypotheses.note: The claim is a comparison of analogy discussions vs solely-abstract discussions. In the formula both coefficients are relative to a neither group (neither analogy nor abstract-only refutation), so no single coefficient equals the A-vs-B contrast; term is null rather than using a conditional coefficient as approximation. hypotheses.note: Word count uses whitespace tokenization of the current argument text only (title excluded). hypotheses.hypothesis: Engaging with a well-reasoned counterargument correlates with a higher frequency of logical concession statements from the original poster in discussions.

right_feature.spec: Read conversation and consider only turns spoken by the OP. Count distinct OP statements that explicitly concede a logical point to a counterargument (e.g., acknowledging a valid flaw, accepting a premise as correct, admitting an argument is sound or that they had not considered something) while not necessarily changing their view. Quoted other-user text is not the OP's own concession unless the OP adopts it. Do not count view-change or delta-award announcements (e.g., 'Δ', 'my view has changed', 'delta awarded'), post-outcome resolution updates or reports of the outcome. Return 0 if the OP has no such statements or no OP turns; null if conversation is missing or malformed. Output a non-negative integer.

left_feature.name: distinct_factual_premises_challenged_count
left_feature.definition: How many distinct factual premises stated in the OP's argument are challenged by the counter-argument comments?
left_feature.spec: Parse OC_comments (JSON list of comments by other users). Read the OP's argument text. Identify the distinct factual (empirical, checkable, non-evaluative) premises asserted by the OP in the argument. Count how many of these distinct premises are directly challenged (disputed, contradicted, or shown to be false/unsupported) by at least one comment in OC_comments. Each premise counts once regardless of how many comments challenge it; one comment challenging several distinct premises counts each. Do not count challenges to values, opinions, or logic that do not dispute a factual claim. Ignore OP view-change/delta-award announcements, post-outcome resolution updates and reports of the outcome in argument or comments as evidence. Comments quoting OP are only challenges if the comment itself disputes the premise. Output a non-negative integer. If OC_comments is a valid empty list, or argument contains no factual premises, output 0; if argument or OC_comments is missing or malformed, output null.

right_feature.spec: Parse OC_comments (JSON list of counter-argument comments by other users). Return 1 if at least one comment contains specific numerical data or statistics (e.g., concrete figures, percentages, rates, dated or measured quantities, study results) used as support for its argument, whether the commenter asserts them or cites an external source for them. Return 0 if no comment does (only general assertions, or numbers that are not data, such as list numbering or incidental counts). Ignore any OP view-change/delta-award announcements, post-outcome resolution updates, or reports of the outcome as evidence. Empty list gives 0; missing or malformed input gives null.

right_feature.spec: Parse OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than the OP).
